title: An abstract nodal completion forces a rational closed point
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $X$ be a scheme locally of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $x\in X$. Write $A=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, let $\mathfrak m$ be its maximal ideal, and let $\widehat A=\varprojlim_{r\ge1}A/\mathfrak m^r$ be its maximal-ideal-adic completion [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion]. Suppose there exists an isomorphism of rings $\widehat A\cong k[[u,v]]/(uv)$ [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series], with no compatibility with the maps from $k$ assumed. Then $x$ is a closed point of $X$ [def-weil-closed-points] and the structure homomorphism $k\to\kappa(x)=A/\mathfrak m$ [def-weil-residue-field] is an isomorphism. In particular, on any affine open neighbourhood $U=\operatorname{Spec}S$ of $x$ for which $S$ is a finitely generated $k$-algebra, its prime $\mathfrak p\subset S$ is maximal and the structure map $k\to S/\mathfrak p$ is an isomorphism. No dimension or separatedness hypothesis is imposed.

proof.text: Put $R=k[[u,v]]/(uv)$. A power series $f$ with constant term $c\ne0$ has inverse $c^{-1}\sum_{j\ge0}(1-c^{-1}f)^j$: each coefficient is a finite sum since $1-c^{-1}f$ has zero constant term [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Thus in $R$ every element with nonzero constant term is a unit, while one with zero constant term cannot be a unit (apply constant-term evaluation). Evaluation $R\twoheadrightarrow k$ therefore has the unique maximal ideal as kernel. Composing $\widehat A\cong R$ with it shows that $\widehat A$ is local with residue field abstractly isomorphic to $k$. The projection $\pi:\widehat A\to A/\mathfrak m$ is surjective: the compatible residues of any lift $a\in A$ map to its class [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion]. Its kernel is maximal, hence the unique maximal ideal. Consequently $L=A/\mathfrak m$ is abstractly isomorphic to $k$. Transporting polynomial coefficients and a root across this field isomorphism shows that $L$ is algebraically closed; this does not identify the structure map $k\to L$.

proof.text: Choose a finite-type affine neighbourhood $U=\operatorname{Spec}S$ of $x$ by [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $\mathfrak p$ be its prime. The germ map identifies $A$ with $S_{\mathfrak p}$ by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-stalk-localization]. The residue extension $L/k$ is therefore the extension at $\mathfrak p$ induced by $k\to S$, and is finitely generated as a FIELD by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-residue-field-extension-finitely-generated], applied to this finite-type map (the prime of $k$ is $(0)$).

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-algclosed-fg-field-finite] to the actual structure homomorphism $k\to L$. Step 1 supplies algebraic closedness of its target, and Step 2 supplies finite field generation. It follows that $L$ is finite-dimensional over $k$ through that map. Since the BASE $k$ is algebraically closed, [lem-weil-pbc-alg-closed-finite-extension-trivial] now makes this specified structure homomorphism bijective.

proof.text: For EVERY finite-type affine neighbourhood $V=\operatorname{Spec}T$ containing $x$, clause (a) of [lem-kun-closed-point-field] applies to $V/k$ with the same finite residue extension $L/k$, so $x$ is closed in $V$ and its prime $\mathfrak q$ is maximal. The affine stalk identification gives $L=T_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak qT_{\mathfrak q}=T/\mathfrak q$, compatibly with $k$, since elements outside a maximal ideal already become units in its field quotient. Thus $k\to T/\mathfrak q$ is an isomorphism. Finally if $z$ specializes $x$ in $X$, choose a finite-type affine neighbourhood $V$ of $z$. An open containing a specialization contains its generalization, so $x\in V$. Closedness of $x$ in $V$ implies $z=x$. Hence $\overline{\{x\}}=\{x\}$ in $X$, proving global closedness without separatedness or quasi-compactness.

source.place: Clause (a); agent-written specialization argument passes from all finite-type affine charts to global closedness.
